opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so what really struck me about supermasks came out of our work trying to understand why the lottery ticket procedure works at all. In the original lottery ticket setup, you train a network, prune the small-magnitude weights, rewind the survivors to their initial values, and retrain. We were poking at each piece of that to see what actually mattered. One surprising thing we found was that if you just take the mask, the pattern of which weights you keep and which you zero out, and apply it to the untrained, randomly initialized network, you already get performance far above chance. On MNIST it was something like 80 or 90 percent accuracy, without ever updating a single weight value.

That was really striking to me, because it suggests that selecting a subnetwork can be a form of learning in its own right. We usually think of training as nudging continuous weight values with gradient descent. But here the information is carried entirely in a binary choice of which connections exist. So we asked whether we could learn the mask directly instead of getting it as a byproduct of pruning. It turns out you can. You put a learnable score on each weight, sample or threshold a binary mask from it, and use a straight-through-style estimator to backprop through that choice. You end up with masks that perform quite well on a completely frozen random network.

The reason I find that interesting as an alternative view of training is a few things. Conceptually, it reframes what a neural network at initialization is. A large random network already contains a huge number of subnetworks, and some of them happen to compute useful functions. Training then looks less like building a function from scratch and more like search or selection. That connects to later work showing that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that match trained ones, and I think it says something about why overparameterization helps.

There are also some practical angles. A binary mask is very cheap to store compared to full-precision weights. If you share one fixed random initialization, say from a seed, you could represent many different tasks just by storing different masks. People have explored that for continual learning, where each task gets its own supermask over the same frozen backbone, so you avoid catastrophic forgetting.

To be clear, I don't think supermasks are about to replace standard training. They're usually not as accurate or as efficient to optimize as just training the weights. But as a lens, they're really useful. They force you to ask what's doing the work in a neural network: the specific values of the weights, or the structure of which connections are active, and especially the signs. We found the signs mattered a lot. For me that kind of question is the most exciting part. It's less about a new training algorithm and more about understanding what learning in these networks actually consists of.

r001.rationale: The response says the magnitude-pruned mask achieves roughly 80–90% accuracy on MNIST when applied to the untrained random network, without updating any weights.

r002.rationale: The response proposes learning or searching for a mask over a frozen, randomly initialized network, describing training as selection among subnetworks rather than weight updates.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing that first grabbed me about Supermasks is how strange the result is when you say it out loud. You take a network with completely random weights, you never update a single one of those weights, and you just learn a binary mask that says "keep this connection, drop that one." And the subnetwork you uncover actually works. On MNIST you can get into the high nineties, and on CIFAR-10 you get well above what you'd expect from a random network. That felt like it shouldn't be possible, and when something shouldn't be possible but is, that's usually where the interesting questions are.

The way we got there was by poking at the lottery ticket hypothesis. Frankle and Carbin had shown that inside a big trained network there are small subnetworks that, if you rewind them to their original initialization, train just as well as the whole thing. Everyone was focused on the training part. What struck us was that if you just applied the winning ticket mask to the untrained network, before any training at all, you already got accuracy way above chance. So the mask itself was carrying information. That pushed us to ask what would happen if you treated the mask as the thing you learn, and left the weights alone entirely. That's the Supermask.

Why do I find it interesting as an alternative to training in the usual sense? A few reasons. One is conceptual. It reframes what "learning" means. Normally we think of training as moving weights through a continuous space. Supermasks suggest that a random initialization is already a kind of overcomplete library, and learning can be selection rather than adjustment. You're not sculpting the function, you're finding it. That connects to older ideas about pruning and to how people think about combinatorial search over architectures, and it hints that initialization and gradient descent are doing more of a joint job than we usually credit.

Another reason is that it changes what you need to store or communicate. If the weights are generated from a seed, then a trained model is just that seed plus one bit per weight. That has obvious appeal for compression and for transmitting models cheaply, but more importantly it tells you something about the information content of training. How many bits does it really take to specify a solution? Supermasks give you a very concrete, if loose, upper bound on that.

And the third reason is more about intuition for optimization. The fact that you can get this far with a binary, non-differentiable object, trained with a fairly crude straight-through style estimator, suggests the loss landscape is far more forgiving than our usual picture of it. There are an enormous number of good solutions nearby, enough that you can hit one by just switching connections on and off. To me that's a window into why overparameterization helps at all.

I want to be honest about the limits. A Supermask on a random network is not competitive with properly training that network, and the gap grows with task difficulty. I don't think anyone should take it as a replacement for gradient descent on weights tomorrow. What I find valuable is that it's a clean, almost minimal experiment that separates two things we normally tangle together, the structure of the network and the values in it, and lets you ask how much each is contributing. Those kinds of probes are how we build a real theory of why deep learning works, and I think we're still pretty short on them.

r002.rationale: The response proposes learning a binary mask over fixed random weights, selecting a working subnetwork without training the model’s weights.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting about supermasks is that they challenge the idea that learning has to mean changing the weights of a neural network. Typically, we randomly initialize a network and then optimize its weights. With supermasks, you keep those random weights fixed and instead learn a mask that selects which connections to retain. And you can get surprisingly good performance just by finding the right subnetwork.

So the randomness isn’t the whole story—the structure you select matters a lot. You’re still learning something, but you’re encoding what you learn in the connectivity rather than in the weight values. That gives us a different way to think about what training is actually doing, and whether weight optimization is the only useful way to find a network that solves a task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think supermasks are interesting because they challenge our usual picture of what it means to train a neural network. Normally, we initialize the weights randomly and then adjust them to solve a task. With a supermask, we keep those random weights fixed and instead learn which connections to keep and which to remove. And you can find subnetworks that perform surprisingly well without ever changing the underlying weights.

So that raises a really interesting question: how much of learning is about finding the right weight values, and how much is about finding the right connectivity? A randomly initialized network may already contain useful structure, and training can be a way of selecting that structure. I wouldn’t say that makes weight training unnecessary, but it gives us a different way to study where a network’s capabilities come from.
